title: Crucial Conversations
author: Kerry Patterson, Joseph Grenny, Ron McMillan, Al Switzler

chapters.title: What's a Crucial Conversation? And Who Cares?
chapters.keys: Learn to spot the talks that matter most, and treat handling them as a skill you can learn, not a gift. A crucial conversation is a talk between two or more people where the stakes are high, opinions differ and emotions run strong. Faced with one, people do one of three things: avoid it, face it and handle it badly, or face it and handle it well. Most handle these talks worst exactly when they matter most, because a body flooded with adrenaline is built for fight or flight, not for careful talk, and the moment usually comes without warning. The authors say getting good at these talks pays off in careers, organizations, relationships and even personal health. They tie this to their research, which found that the people others look to as most influential at work are the ones who handle these talks well. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: the authors' research with organizations, in which they looked for the people coworkers named as most influential and found that what set them apart was their skill at crucial conversations.

chapters.title: Mastering Crucial Conversations: The Power of Dialogue
chapters.keys: Aim for dialogue, which is the free flow of meaning between two or more people, and get every relevant fact, opinion and feeling into the open. The authors' picture for this is the pool of shared meaning: each person brings their own opinions, feelings, theories and experiences, and dialogue fills a shared pool with them. When people do not feel safe, they stop adding to the pool and slip into silence, which means holding meaning back, or violence, which means forcing meaning into the pool or trying to make others accept it. The authors say a fuller pool works because it leads to smarter decisions. It also works because people who helped fill the pool act on the decision with unity and conviction instead of resistance. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Kevin, a vice president whom his peers named as unusually influential, sat in an executive meeting where the CEO pushed for a move to new offices outside the decision process the team had agreed on. While the other executives kept quiet, Kevin raised it candidly and respectfully, and so got the real issue on the table.

chapters.title: Start with Heart: How to Stay Focused on What You Really Want
chapters.keys: Work on yourself first, because you are the only person you can directly control. Start with heart, which means staying focused on what you really want. Ask yourself what you want for yourself, what you want for the other person and what you want for the relationship. Then ask how you would behave if you really wanted those things. Watch for the moment your motive shifts to winning, punishing the other person or keeping the peace, and steer back to your real goal. Refuse the Fool's Choice, the belief that you must pick between telling the truth and keeping a friend. Search instead for an and: name what you want, name what you do not want, and ask how you could get both. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Greta, a CEO who was pressing her company to cut costs, was challenged in public about the money spent remodeling her own office. She felt the urge to defend herself, stopped to ask what she really wanted, then thanked the person who raised it and admitted the apparent hypocrisy.

chapters.title: Learn to Look: How to Notice When Safety Is at Risk
chapters.keys: While you talk, watch two things at once: the content of the conversation, and the conditions, meaning how people are acting and whether they feel safe. Learn to spot the moment a talk turns crucial from signals in your body, your emotions and your behavior. Watch for safety problems. Silence shows up as masking, avoiding and withdrawing. Violence shows up as controlling, labeling and attacking. Watch yourself as well. The authors offer their Style Under Stress test so you can see which of these moves you fall into. Their reason: silence and violence are signs that people no longer feel safe, and catching those signs early lets you restore safety before the talk falls apart. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: none recalled with confidence.

chapters.title: Make It Safe: How to Make It Safe to Talk about Almost Anything
chapters.keys: When safety breaks down, step out of the content, make it safe, then step back in. People rarely get defensive over the content itself. They get defensive because they stop feeling safe, and the authors say that once safety is restored you can talk about almost anything. Safety rests on two conditions. Mutual purpose means the others believe you care about their goals and are working toward a shared outcome. Mutual respect means they believe you respect them as people. Learn to tell which of the two is at risk, then use these tools. Apologize when you have truly done something wrong. Contrast to fix a misunderstanding: say what you do not intend, then what you do intend. Use CRIB to build mutual purpose, in this order: Commit to seek mutual purpose, Recognize the purpose behind the strategy each person is pushing, Invent a mutual purpose, and Brainstorm new strategies. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Yvonne and Jotham, a married couple who disagree about how often to be intimate. Working through the CRIB steps, they find that each of them wants to feel loved and appreciated, and they start brainstorming ways of being together that work for both.

chapters.title: Master My Stories: How to Stay in Dialogue When You're Angry, Scared, or Hurt
chapters.keys: Your emotions do not just happen to you. You create them with the stories you tell about what you see and hear, so you can change them by telling a different story. The authors call this sequence the Path to Action: you see and hear something, tell yourself a story about it, feel an emotion, then act. To master your stories, retrace your path in this order: notice your behavior, get in touch with your feelings, analyze your story, and get back to the facts. Watch for three clever stories. A victim story says it's not my fault. A villain story says it's all your fault. A helpless story says there's nothing else I can do. Then tell the rest of the story. Turn victims into actors by asking what part you played. Turn villains into humans by asking why a reasonable, decent person would act this way. Turn the helpless into the able by asking what you really want and what you would do right now if you wanted it. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Maria, a copywriter, whose coworker Louis talked with the boss about their joint project without her and then did most of the talking when they presented it. She told herself he didn't trust her, felt angry, and swung between silence and sarcastic jabs.

chapters.title: STATE My Path: How to Speak Persuasively, Not Abrasively
chapters.keys: When you have something hard or risky to say, speak in a way that is both honest and safe by using STATE. The first three steps are what you say: Share your facts, Tell your story, and Ask for others' paths, meaning their facts and stories. The last two are how you say it: Talk tentatively, stating your story as a story rather than as fact, and Encourage testing, making it safe for others to disagree. Start with facts because, the authors say, facts are the least controversial, the most persuasive and the least insulting part of your view. The stronger your belief, the more you must guard against pushing it harder, because pushing makes others resist. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Carole finds a charge from the Good Night Motel, close to home, on the credit card bill and concludes that her husband Bob is having an affair. The authors compare accusing him outright with opening with the charge as a fact, then voicing her worry and giving him room to explain.

chapters.title: Explore Others' Paths: How to Listen When Others Blow Up or Clam Up
chapters.keys: When others clam up or blow up, start with heart: be curious and patient, and go after their path back to its source, the facts and story driving their feelings. Use AMPP, in this order. Ask, to show interest in their view. Mirror, to name the emotions you see in their tone and face. Paraphrase, to restate their story in your own words. Prime, to offer your best guess at what they think when they still hold back. The authors say this works because people act out of their own stories, and sincere listening makes it safe for them to put those stories in the pool. When it is your turn to respond, use ABC. Agree where you do agree. Build on what they left out. Compare, rather than call them wrong, where you differ. Understanding their view does not mean you agree with it. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Wendy, a teenage daughter, starts dating Doug, who worries her parent, and when the parent scolds her she blows up and withdraws. The parent apologizes and uses Ask, Mirror, Paraphrase and Prime to draw her out until she admits she has felt unnoticed and that Doug has paid her attention, and the real issue comes into the open.

chapters.title: Move to Action: How to Turn Crucial Conversations into Action and Results
chapters.keys: Dialogue is not decision making. Once the pool is full, turn shared meaning into action. Decide how you will decide, using one of four methods. Command means decisions are made without involving others. Consult means you gather input, then one person or a small group decides. Vote means an agreed share of the group carries the decision. Consensus means everyone must honestly agree. To choose a method, ask four questions: who cares, who knows, who must agree, and how many people it is worth involving. Finish clearly: settle who does what by when and how you will follow up, write it down, and hold people to it. The authors say unclear decisions and vague assignments leave people with violated expectations and work that never gets done. Reversal: they warn against using consensus for everything and save it for high-stakes, complex issues. Story the author tells: Cara and Rene agree that a cruise is a good idea; Rene then picks a particular cruise and pays the deposit, and Cara is upset because she agreed to a cruise in principle, not to that one.

chapters.title: Yeah, But: Advice for Tough Cases
chapters.keys: When you think yeah, but my case is different, the authors answer that their skills still apply. This chapter works through the tough cases people raise and shows how the same tools fit each one. Among them are harassment, an oversensitive partner, a coworker who does not keep commitments, a deeply personal issue like hygiene, and someone you do not trust. For each case they point to the particular skills that fit it, such as Contrasting (saying what you don't mean before saying what you do) and building a shared purpose. On trust, they say you do not need to trust someone in everything to hold a dialogue on the issue in front of you. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: none recalled with confidence.
